Covariance and correlation, for programmers

Sample covariance and its units, the Pearson correlation as the covariance of the z's and as a cosine (with Cauchy-Schwarz for ), the covariance matrix and its role in PCA, slope and r² of the regression, what r doesn't see (Anscombe, curves, outliers) with Spearman and Kendall, the uncertainty of r with small samples, confounding, partial correlation and multicollinearity, and numerically stable computation. With a from-scratch module verified against NumPy, SciPy and pandas, a simulated fleet and a worked example by hand.

Summary

  • Sample covariance : interpretable sign, magnitude in units of times units of . np.cov and pandas use ; np.var, .
  • is the covariance of the z's and the cosine between the centered vectors; by Cauchy-Schwarz, , with equality only if the points lie on a line.
  • In simple regression, slope and . The matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite; its eigenvectors are the PCA components.
  • r measures linear association and is fragile against outliers: Spearman (Pearson of the ranks) and Kendall measure monotonic association and are robust. Independence ⇒ , not the other way around.
  • With small n, r is very noisy: . With many pairs, spurious correlations appear.
  • Correlation is not causation: confounding (partial correlation), selection, reverse causation. To compute, use two passes or Welford, never .

§1 · Covariance

Mean of products of deviations

For two random variables, the covariance is the expectation of the product of their deviations; its sample estimator divides by for the same reason as the variance in topic 7 (the sample means use up one degree of freedom, and this way the estimator is unbiased):

Each term is the signed area of the rectangle between and the point: positive in quadrants I and III, negative in II and IV. Properties that get used all the time:

The second one is the units problem: switching from tonnes to kilograms multiplies the covariance by 1,000 without changing anything about the relationship. The third one explains, for example, why the total consumption of two legs of a route varies more than their separate variances would suggest if the legs move together (same driver, same wind). Watch out for the library conventions:

calldivides bynotes
np.cov(x, y)returns the 2×2 matrix; bias=True or ddof=0 for ; with a matrix, rows = variables unless rowvar=False
np.corrcoef(X)—r doesn't depend on versus ; same rowvar
DataFrame.cov() / .corr()columns = variables; drops NaN pairwise; method="spearman"|"kendall"
np.var(x) / np.std(x)unlike Series.var(), which uses !
scipy.stats.pearsonr—r, p-value and interval (.confidence_interval())

basico.py · the 8 trucks from the simple version · actual output

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sim import CARGA8 as x, CONSUMO8 as y        # 8 trucks: tonnes and L/100 km

dx, dy = x - x.mean(), y - y.mean()
c = np.sum(dx * dy) / (len(x) - 1)
r = c / (x.std(ddof=1) * y.std(ddof=1))
print("cov", round(c, 4), " r", round(r, 4), " cov in kg", round(np.cov(x * 1000, y)[0, 1], 1), " r in kg", round(np.corrcoef(x * 1000, y)[0, 1], 4))
zx, zy = dx / x.std(ddof=1), dy / y.std(ddof=1)
print("mean of zx·zy (n − 1)", round(np.sum(zx * zy) / 7, 4), " cosine(dx, dy)", round(dx @ dy / np.linalg.norm(dx) / np.linalg.norm(dy), 4))
b = c / x.var(ddof=1)
print("slope", round(b, 4), " = r·sy/sx", round(r * y.std(ddof=1) / x.std(ddof=1), 4), " r²", round(r**2, 4), " polyfit", np.polyfit(x, y, 1).round(4))
# each library's ddof conventions
print("np.cov", round(np.cov(x, y)[0, 1], 4), " np.cov(bias=True)", round(np.cov(x, y, bias=True)[0, 1], 4),
      " pandas", round(pd.Series(x).cov(pd.Series(y)), 4), " np.var", round(np.var(x), 4), " pd.var", round(pd.Series(x).var(), 4))

# cov 18.5714  r 0.9231  cov in kg 18571.4  r in kg 0.9231
# mean of zx·zy (n − 1) 0.9231  cosine(dx, dy) 0.9231
# slope 0.4851  = r·sy/sx 0.4851  r² 0.8522  polyfit [ 0.4851 24.7239]
# np.cov 18.5714  np.cov(bias=True) 16.25  pandas 18.5714  np.var 33.5  pd.var 38.2857

Mixing np.var (33.5) with np.cov (which uses 38.29 on the diagonal) gives a slightly wrong r: a typical mistake when computing the slope or the correlation by hand.

§2 · Correlation

Covariance of the z's, cosine and Cauchy-Schwarz

Dividing by the two standard deviations makes the units disappear:

With the centered vectors and , the cancel out and what's left is the cosine from topic 2:

The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is an equality only if : if and only if all the points lie on a line (neither horizontal nor vertical). The one-line proof: for all is a degree-2 polynomial in without two real roots, so its discriminant is .

r is invariant under with (with it flips sign): that's why scaling doesn't change correlations. And it connects directly with simple least-squares linear regression:

In z, the line has slope exactly : if a truck is 1σ from the mean load, its consumption is predicted to be only σ from the mean consumption. This is Galton's regression to the mean. And there isn't just one line: regressing on gives slope , which in the plane is ; the two lines coincide only if .

§3 · Matrices

The covariance matrix and the correlation matrix

With columns in a matrix (rows = trucks) and centered by column:

is symmetric and positive semidefinite: for any weight vector ,

That identity is the variance of any linear combination of columns (for example, the total cost ). If a column is an exact linear combination of others, is singular; if it almost is, it is ill-conditioned (§6).

PCA diagonalizes (topic 5): the columns of are directions uncorrelated with each other and is the variance of the data along each one. With , the columns with the most numerical variance (the km, in thousands) dominate; with (equivalent to standardizing first), they all weigh the same. In the fleet (§9), the first eigenvalue of with the 7 real columns is 3.19: 46% of the total variance lies in a single direction, the km-liters-dollars block. The same matrices appear in the Mahalanobis distance, in the multivariate normal and in the Kalman filter.

§4 · What r doesn't see

Anscombe, curves, outliers, Spearman and Kendall

r sums up the cloud in a number that only measures fit to a line. Anscombe's quartet (1973) is four datasets with the same means, variances, r = 0.816 and regression line, and completely different shapes. Two alternatives based on order:

Spearman is Pearson on the ranks (with ties, average rank), and it equals 1 for any strictly increasing relationship, even a curved one. Kendall counts concordant pairs of points (: both order them the same way) and discordant ones (); and are the pairs tied in each variable. Its interpretation is direct: is, without ties, the probability that two random trucks are in the same order in both columns. Neither of them sees the U: for that you need a general dependence measure, like Székely's distance correlation (which is 0 only under independence) or mutual information.

And the relationship with the independence of topic 9: if and are independent, and the covariance is 0. Not the other way around: with and , and yet is determined by . The well-known exception: if is bivariate normal, covariance 0 does imply independence.

§5 · Uncertainty

How much r moves with small n, and the hunt for correlations

Under the hypothesis with normal data, the statistic

gives the p-value of pearsonr. For intervals, the distribution of is skewed near ±1; Fisher (1915) stabilizes it with

The figures in the table come from incert.py. With 15 trucks, an r of 0.5 isn't even "significant" and its interval runs from −0.02 to 0.81. And with many pairs the problem multiplies: with 9 columns of pure noise and 15 rows (36 pairs), the median of the largest in the table is 0.60, and in 85% of the tables some pair comes out with p < 0.05. It is the correlation version of multiple comparisons: correct with Bonferroni () or with Benjamini-Hochberg, and above all confirm on new data what you found by searching.

nminimum |r| for p < 0.0595% CI if r = 0.5

incert.py · actual output

import math
import numpy as np
from cor import pearson, p_valor_r, ic_fisher, matriz_corr
from sim import CARGA8, CONSUMO8

r = pearson(CARGA8, CONSUMO8); n = 8
t = r * math.sqrt((n - 2) / (1 - r * r))
print(f"8 trucks: r = {r:.4f}  t = {t:.3f}  p = {p_valor_r(r, n):.5f}  Fisher 95% CI = [{ic_fisher(r, n)[0]:.3f}, {ic_fisher(r, n)[1]:.3f}]")
# critical r (p = 0.05, two-sided) by n, and interval width for r = 0.5
for m in (8, 15, 30, 100, 500):
    lo, hi = 0.0, 0.999
    for _ in range(60):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2; lo, hi = (mid, hi) if p_valor_r(mid, m) > 0.05 else (lo, mid)
    a, b = ic_fisher(0.5, m)
    print(f"n = {m:3d}: |r| > {hi:.3f} for p < 0.05;  r = 0.5 → 95% CI [{a:.2f}, {b:.2f}]")
# many pairs of columns with no relationship at all: 9 columns (36 pairs), 15 trucks
rng = np.random.default_rng(3); mx = []; alguna = 0
for _ in range(20_000):
    R = matriz_corr(rng.normal(size=(15, 9))); v = np.abs(R[np.triu_indices(9, 1)])
    mx.append(v.max()); alguna += np.any(v > 0.514)
mx = np.array(mx)
print(f"9 noise columns, 15 rows: median max |r| {np.median(mx):.2f}; in {np.mean(mx > 0.5):.0%} of the tables some |r| > 0.5;"
      f" some 'significant' (p < 0.05) in {alguna / 20_000:.0%}; expected with no dependence 1 − 0.95^36 = {1 - 0.95**36:.0%}")

# n =  15: |r| > 0.514 for p < 0.05;  r = 0.5 → 95% CI [-0.02, 0.81]

# n = 100: |r| > 0.197 for p < 0.05;  r = 0.5 → 95% CI [0.34, 0.63]

§6 · Causation

Confounding, partial correlation, selection and multicollinearity

Confounding. If a variable influences and , it induces a correlation between them even if they don't influence each other. In the fleet, the route type (city or highway) decides which trucks go to the city (the old ones) and how much they burn: . The partial correlation removes from and what explains linearly and correlates the residuals; with a single :

With and it gives : given the route, age says nothing about consumption. A relationship that changes sign when you condition is Simpson's paradox. Partial correlation only removes the confounders that are measured and act linearly; causation requires a model of what causes what (a causal graph, Pearl's backdoor criterion) or a randomized experiment.

Selection. Filtering on a consequence of both variables creates correlation (Berkson's bias): if the only trucks that reach the analysis are those that went through an audit for "high consumption or many breakdowns", in that sample the two appear negatively correlated even though they are independent in the fleet. Reverse causation: breakdowns cause visits to the maintenance shop, not the other way around. Common trends: two time series that grow (fleet km and insurance price) have a high r because they share a trend; correlate the differences, not the levels.

Multicollinearity. In a regression with several columns, if one is almost a linear combination of the others, its coefficient has a huge variance. It is measured with the variance inflation factor, which is the diagonal of :

with the one from regressing column on the rest. Above 10 is usually considered serious. In the fleet, liters and dollars (r = 0.998) give VIFs of 244 and 230; removing the dollars brings them down to 20, because liters are still almost km × consumption. The way out: remove redundant columns, combine them (PCA) or regularize (ridge spreads the weight across collinear columns).

§7 · Stable computation

Never Σxy − n·x̄·ȳ

The one-pass formula subtracts two huge, nearly equal numbers when the means are large compared with the spread: timestamps in milliseconds () and odometers ( km). The two-pass version centers first; if the data arrives as a stream, Welford updates the means and the co-moment without large subtractions, and Chan, Golub and LeVeque merge summaries of chunks (per truck, per day, per Spark partition):

estable.py · actual output

import numpy as np
from cor import covarianza, CovOnline

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
t = 1.7e12 + np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 600_000, 2000))           # Unix timestamps in ms (10 minutes)
km = 512_345.0 + 2e-5 * (t - t[0]) + rng.normal(0, 0.05, 2000)  # odometer (km): 72 km/h
ref = np.cov(t - t[0], km - km[0])[0, 1]                       # reference: shifted data in float64
n = len(t)
ingenua = (np.sum(t * km) - n * t.mean() * km.mean()) / (n - 1)    # Σxy − n·x̄·ȳ
o = CovOnline()
for a, b in zip(t, km): o.add(a, b)
for nombre, v in [("Σxy − n·x̄·ȳ", ingenua), ("two-pass", covarianza(t, km)), ("Welford online", o.cov()), ("np.cov", np.cov(t, km)[0, 1])]:
    print(f"{nombre:18s} {v:16.3f}   relative error {abs(v - ref) / abs(ref):.1e}")
t32, k32 = t.astype(np.float32), km.astype(np.float32)
d32 = ((t - t[0]).astype(np.float32), (km - km[0]).astype(np.float32))
print("float32 direct:", f"{abs(np.cov(t32, k32)[0, 1] - ref) / ref:.1e}",
      "  float32 after subtracting the first value in float64:", f"{abs(np.cov(*d32)[0, 1] - ref) / ref:.1e}")

# Σxy − n·x̄·ȳ             593266.361   relative error 1.9e-04
# two-pass                 593152.225   relative error 5.9e-16
# Welford online           593152.232   relative error 1.2e-08
# np.cov                   593152.225   relative error 9.8e-16
# float32 direct: 6.2e-03   float32 after subtracting the first value in float64: 1.6e-09

The naive formula loses 12 orders of magnitude of precision compared with two passes, and in direct float32 the times can't even be told apart (a float32 near only has a resolution of about 131 s). Subtracting an origin in float64 before converting fixes it: that's what you should do with timestamps and GPS coordinates before any variance computation.

§8 · From scratch

Covariances, correlations, p-values and streaming, verified

cor.py

"""Covariance and correlation from scratch (numpy and the standard library only)."""
import math
from statistics import NormalDist
import numpy as np


def covarianza(x, y, ddof=1):
    """Two passes: first the means, then the mean of the products of the deviations."""
    x = np.asarray(x, float); y = np.asarray(y, float)
    return float(np.sum((x - x.mean()) * (y - y.mean())) / (len(x) - ddof))


def pearson(x, y):
    x = np.asarray(x, float); y = np.asarray(y, float)
    dx, dy = x - x.mean(), y - y.mean()
    return float(np.sum(dx * dy) / math.sqrt(np.sum(dx * dx) * np.sum(dy * dy)))   # cosine of dx and dy


def rangos(x):
    """Ranks 1..n; ties get the mean of their ranks."""
    x = np.asarray(x, float); o = np.argsort(x, kind="mergesort"); xs = x[o]
    r = np.empty(len(x)); i = 0
    while i < len(x):
        j = i
        while j + 1 < len(x) and xs[j + 1] == xs[i]:
            j += 1
        r[o[i:j + 1]] = (i + j) / 2 + 1; i = j + 1
    return r


def spearman(x, y):
    return pearson(rangos(x), rangos(y))


def kendall_tau_b(x, y):
    """(concordant − discordant) / sqrt((n0 − n1)(n0 − n2)); O(n²), enough for thousands of rows."""
    x = np.asarray(x, float); y = np.asarray(y, float); n = len(x)
    i, j = np.triu_indices(n, 1)
    s = np.sign(x[i] - x[j]) * np.sign(y[i] - y[j])
    n0 = n * (n - 1) / 2; tx = np.sum(x[i] == x[j]); ty = np.sum(y[i] == y[j])
    return float(np.sum(s) / math.sqrt((n0 - tx) * (n0 - ty)))


def matriz_cov(X, ddof=1):
    """Rows = observations, columns = variables: Xcᵀ Xc / (n − 1)."""
    X = np.asarray(X, float); Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
    return Xc.T @ Xc / (len(X) - ddof)


def matriz_corr(X):
    S = matriz_cov(X); d = np.sqrt(np.diag(S))
    R = S / np.outer(d, d); np.fill_diagonal(R, 1.0)
    return R


def correlacion_parcial(x, y, z):
    """r of x and y after removing what z (one or several columns) explains linearly."""
    Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), np.asarray(z, float)])
    res = lambda v: v - Z @ np.linalg.lstsq(Z, v, rcond=None)[0]
    return pearson(res(np.asarray(x, float)), res(np.asarray(y, float)))


def _betacf(a, b, x, it=300, eps=1e-15):
    """Continued fraction of the incomplete beta (Numerical Recipes, §6.4)."""
    qab, qap, qam = a + b, a + 1, a - 1
    c, d = 1.0, 1 - qab * x / qap
    d = 1 / (d if abs(d) > 1e-300 else 1e-300); h = d
    for m in range(1, it + 1):
        m2 = 2 * m
        for aa in (m * (b - m) * x / ((qam + m2) * (a + m2)), -(a + m) * (qab + m) * x / ((a + m2) * (qap + m2))):
            d = 1 + aa * d; d = 1 / (d if abs(d) > 1e-300 else 1e-300)
            c = 1 + aa / c; c = c if abs(c) > 1e-300 else 1e-300
            h *= d * c
        if abs(d * c - 1) < eps:
            break
    return h


def beta_inc(a, b, x):
    """Regularized incomplete beta I_x(a, b)."""
    if x <= 0: return 0.0
    if x >= 1: return 1.0
    lb = math.lgamma(a + b) - math.lgamma(a) - math.lgamma(b) + a * math.log(x) + b * math.log1p(-x)
    if x < (a + 1) / (a + b + 2):
        return math.exp(lb) * _betacf(a, b, x) / a
    return 1 - math.exp(lb) * _betacf(b, a, 1 - x) / b


def p_valor_r(r, n):
    """Test of ρ = 0 (two-sided): t = r·sqrt((n − 2)/(1 − r²)) follows a Student's t with n − 2 d.f."""
    df = n - 2; t2 = r * r * df / (1 - r * r)
    return beta_inc(df / 2, 0.5, df / (df + t2))


def ic_fisher(r, n, conf=0.95):
    """Interval for ρ with Fisher's transformation: atanh(r) ≈ normal with std. dev. 1/sqrt(n − 3)."""
    z = NormalDist().inv_cdf((1 + conf) / 2); h = z / math.sqrt(n - 3)
    return math.tanh(math.atanh(r) - h), math.tanh(math.atanh(r) + h)


def vif(X):
    """Variance inflation factor of each column: 1 / (1 − R²_j) = diagonal of the inverse of R."""
    return np.diag(np.linalg.inv(matriz_corr(X)))


class CovOnline:
    """One-pass covariance (Welford) and merging of two summaries (Chan, Golub and LeVeque)."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.n = 0; self.mx = 0.0; self.my = 0.0; self.C = 0.0; self.Sx = 0.0; self.Sy = 0.0

    def add(self, x, y):
        dx, dy = x - self.mx, y - self.my                  # deviations from the old means
        self.n += 1; self.mx += dx / self.n; self.my += dy / self.n
        self.C += dx * (y - self.my)                       # old × new: exact, no large subtractions
        self.Sx += dx * (x - self.mx); self.Sy += dy * (y - self.my)
        return self

    def merge(self, o):
        n = self.n + o.n; dx, dy = o.mx - self.mx, o.my - self.my; f = self.n * o.n / n
        self.C += o.C + dx * dy * f; self.Sx += o.Sx + dx * dx * f; self.Sy += o.Sy + dy * dy * f
        self.mx += dx * o.n / n; self.my += dy * o.n / n; self.n = n
        return self

    def cov(self): return self.C / (self.n - 1)
    def corr(self): return self.C / math.sqrt(self.Sx * self.Sy)

check.py · 300 random problems (n from 5 to 200, a third with ties) · actual output

"""Compares cor.py with numpy, pandas and scipy on 300 random problems (with ties)."""
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from cor import *

rng = np.random.default_rng(0); err = {}
def up(k, v): err[k] = max(err.get(k, 0.0), float(v))
for t in range(300):
    n = int(rng.integers(5, 200)); rho = rng.uniform(-0.95, 0.95)
    x = rng.normal(size=n); y = rho * x + np.sqrt(1 - rho**2) * rng.normal(size=n)
    if t % 3 == 0: x, y = np.round(x, 1), np.round(y, 1)          # ties
    X = np.column_stack([x, y, rng.normal(size=n), x**2])
    up("covarianza vs np.cov", abs(covarianza(x, y) - np.cov(x, y)[0, 1]))
    up("matriz_cov vs np.cov", np.abs(matriz_cov(X) - np.cov(X.T)).max())
    up("matriz_corr vs np.corrcoef / DataFrame.corr", max(np.abs(matriz_corr(X) - np.corrcoef(X.T)).max(), np.abs(matriz_corr(X) - pd.DataFrame(X).corr().values).max()))
    pr = stats.pearsonr(x, y); r = pearson(x, y)
    up("pearson vs scipy.stats.pearsonr", abs(r - pr.statistic))
    up("p_valor_r vs pearsonr().pvalue (relative)", abs(p_valor_r(r, n) - pr.pvalue) / max(pr.pvalue, 1e-300))
    lo, hi = ic_fisher(r, n); ci = pr.confidence_interval(0.95)
    up("ic_fisher vs pearsonr().confidence_interval", max(abs(lo - ci.low), abs(hi - ci.high)))
    up("rangos vs scipy.stats.rankdata", np.abs(rangos(x) - stats.rankdata(x)).max())
    up("spearman vs spearmanr / corr('spearman')", max(abs(spearman(x, y) - stats.spearmanr(x, y).statistic), abs(spearman(x, y) - pd.Series(x).corr(pd.Series(y), method="spearman"))))
    up("kendall_tau_b vs kendalltau / corr('kendall')", max(abs(kendall_tau_b(x, y) - stats.kendalltau(x, y).statistic), abs(kendall_tau_b(x, y) - pd.Series(x).corr(pd.Series(y), method="kendall"))))
    z = X[:, 2]; a = np.c_[np.ones(n), z]
    rx = x - a @ np.linalg.lstsq(a, x, rcond=None)[0]; ry = y - a @ np.linalg.lstsq(a, y, rcond=None)[0]
    rxy, rxz, ryz = np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1], np.corrcoef(x, z)[0, 1], np.corrcoef(y, z)[0, 1]
    up("correlacion_parcial vs 3-r formula", abs(correlacion_parcial(x, y, z) - (rxy - rxz * ryz) / np.sqrt((1 - rxz**2) * (1 - ryz**2))))
    # online, in chunks and merging
    parts = np.array_split(np.arange(n), 3); tot = CovOnline()
    for p in parts:
        c = CovOnline()
        for i in p: c.add(x[i], y[i])
        tot.merge(c)                                   # merging with an empty summary works too
    up("CovOnline (3 merged chunks) vs np.cov / corrcoef", max(abs(tot.cov() - np.cov(x, y)[0, 1]), abs(tot.corr() - np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])))
    Xv = X[:, :3]
    A = np.c_[np.ones(n), Xv[:, 1:]]; res = Xv[:, 0] - A @ np.linalg.lstsq(A, Xv[:, 0], rcond=None)[0]
    up("vif vs 1/(1 − R²) via regression", abs(vif(Xv)[0] - 1 / (np.sum(res**2) / np.sum((Xv[:, 0] - Xv[:, 0].mean())**2))))
w = max(len(k) for k in err)
for k, v in err.items(): print(f"# {k:{w}s}  {v:.1e}")

# covarianza vs np.cov                              6.7e-16
# matriz_cov vs np.cov                              8.9e-16
# matriz_corr vs np.corrcoef / DataFrame.corr       8.9e-16
# pearson vs scipy.stats.pearsonr                   4.4e-16
# p_valor_r vs pearsonr().pvalue (relative)         4.7e-13
# ic_fisher vs pearsonr().confidence_interval       8.9e-16
# rangos vs scipy.stats.rankdata                    0.0e+00
# spearman vs spearmanr / corr('spearman')          2.2e-16
# kendall_tau_b vs kendalltau / corr('kendall')     2.2e-16
# correlacion_parcial vs 3-r formula                7.8e-16
# CovOnline (3 merged chunks) vs np.cov / corrcoef  8.9e-16
# vif vs 1/(1 − R²) via regression                  5.3e-14

Details for matching the libraries: ranks with ties use the average rank (rankdata(method="average")), which is what spearmanr and pandas do; kendalltau returns the variant by default, corrected for ties; the interval of pearsonr().confidence_interval() is Fisher's; and the p-value via Student's t matches SciPy's up to rounding errors in the incomplete beta (relative errors of , also for tiny p-values).

§9 · In the fleet

500 trucks, 9 columns and a confounding variable

The simulator generates the monthly table from idea 6 of the simple version (with two columns of pure chance), the 240 trucks from idea 5 (age, route type and consumption) and the two outlier scenarios from idea 4.

sim.py

"""Simulated fleet for topic 10 (covariance and correlation). Everything with fixed seeds."""
import numpy as np

# The 8 trucks of the worked example: average load (t) and consumption (L/100 km)
CARGA8 = np.array([6, 9, 11, 14, 16, 19, 21, 24], float)
CONSUMO8 = np.array([27, 30, 29, 33, 31, 35, 36, 35], float)


def juguete(n=120, seed=10):
    """Four pairs of fleet columns (one truck per row, one month of data)."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    carga = r.uniform(4, 26, n)
    consumo = 24 + 0.5 * carga + r.normal(0, 2.6, n)
    ralenti = r.uniform(5, 80, n)                                   # idling hours per month
    gasto = 3900 + 4.1 * ralenti + r.normal(0, 140, n)              # $ of diesel per month
    exper = r.uniform(1, 30, n)                                     # driver's years of experience
    frenadas = np.clip(9 - 0.18 * exper + r.normal(0, 1.6, n), 0.2, None)   # harsh braking events per 1,000 km
    dia = r.integers(1, 31, n).astype(float)                        # day of the month of the refuel
    consumo2 = 32 + r.normal(0, 2.4, n)
    return dict(carga=(carga, consumo), ralenti=(ralenti, gasto), exper=(exper, frenadas), dia=(dia, consumo2))


def velocidad(n=160, seed=13):
    """Average trip speed (km/h) and consumption: U-shaped curve with its minimum at 50 km/h."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    v = r.uniform(10, 90, n)
    c = 29 + 0.005 * (v - 50) ** 2 + r.normal(0, 1.2, n)
    return v, c


def atipico(n=20, seed=33):
    """Two clouds of 20 trucks: no relationship (driver age and consumption) and with a relationship (load and consumption)."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    edad = r.uniform(24, 60, n)
    cons = 32 + r.normal(0, 1.6, n)
    carga = r.uniform(6, 24, n)
    cons2 = 24 + 0.5 * carga + r.normal(0, 1.4, n)
    return (edad, cons), (carga, cons2)


def confusion(n=240, seed=13):
    """Truck age, route type (1 = city) and consumption. The route decides consumption; age decides the route."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    edad = r.uniform(1, 15, n)
    ciudad = (r.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(edad - 8) / 1.6))).astype(int)
    cons = np.where(ciudad == 1, 37.5, 30.0) + r.normal(0, 1.8, n)
    return edad, ciudad, cons


NOMBRES = ["km in the month", "liters", "diesel $", "average load", "idling", "truck age",
           "harsh braking events", "license plate letter", "driver's birth day"]


def flota(n=500, seed=14):
    """Monthly table of n trucks with 9 columns (the last two are pure chance)."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    km = r.uniform(4000, 12000, n)
    carga = r.uniform(6, 24, n)
    edad = r.uniform(1, 15, n)
    ralenti = np.clip(20 + 2.2 * edad + r.normal(0, 12, n), 2, None)
    l100 = 24 + 0.5 * carga + 0.25 * edad + r.normal(0, 2.0, n)
    litros = km * l100 / 100 + 2.5 * ralenti
    euros = litros * r.normal(1.65, 0.03, n)
    frenadas = np.clip(6 - 0.00025 * km + r.normal(0, 1.2, n), 0.1, None)
    letra = r.integers(1, 27, n).astype(float)
    nac = r.integers(1, 32, n).astype(float)
    X = np.column_stack([km, litros, euros, carga, ralenti, edad, frenadas, letra, nac])
    return X

flota.py · actual output

import numpy as np
from sim import flota, confusion, atipico, NOMBRES
from cor import matriz_corr, matriz_cov, pearson, spearman, correlacion_parcial, vif

X = flota(); R = matriz_corr(X)
iu = np.triu_indices(9, 1); o = np.argsort(-np.abs(R[iu]))[:4]
print("most correlated pairs:", [(NOMBRES[iu[0][k]], NOMBRES[iu[1][k]], round(float(R[iu][k]), 3)) for k in o])
print("VIF km, liters, $, load, idling, age:", vif(X[:, :6]).round(1))
print("VIF without the $:                   ", vif(X[:, [0, 1, 3, 4, 5]]).round(1))
w, V = np.linalg.eigh(R[:7, :7]); print("eigenvalues of R (7 real columns):", w[::-1].round(2), " variance explained by the 1st:", f"{w[-1] / 7:.0%}")
S = matriz_cov(X[:, :3]); print("covariances km/liters/$ (different scales): diagonal", np.diag(S).round(0))

edad, ciudad, cons = confusion()
print(f"age and consumption: r {pearson(edad, cons):+.3f};  partial given route {correlacion_parcial(edad, cons, ciudad):+.3f};"
      f"  r(age, city) {pearson(edad, ciudad):+.3f}  r(city, consumption) {pearson(ciudad, cons):+.3f}")
(a, b), (x, y) = atipico()
for nombre, p, q, (ox, oy) in [("no relationship", a, b, (72, 52)), ("with relationship", x, y, (27, 21))]:
    P, Q = np.r_[p, ox], np.r_[q, oy]
    print(f"outlier, {nombre}: r {pearson(p, q):+.3f} → {pearson(P, Q):+.3f};  Spearman {spearman(p, q):+.3f} → {spearman(P, Q):+.3f}")
R15 = matriz_corr(X[:15]); ruido = [(i, j) for i, j in zip(*iu) if j >= 7]
k = max(ruido, key=lambda t: abs(R15[t])); print(f"15 trucks: {NOMBRES[k[0]]} / {NOMBRES[k[1]]} r = {R15[k]:+.2f} (500 trucks: {R[k]:+.2f})")

# most correlated pairs: [('liters', 'diesel $', 0.998), ('km in the month', 'liters', 0.933), ('km in the month', 'diesel $', 0.932), ('idling', 'truck age', 0.596)]
# VIF km, liters, $, load, idling, age: [ 18.9 244.  229.6   2.4   1.6   1.7]
# VIF without the $:                    [18.9 20.2  2.4  1.6  1.7]
# eigenvalues of R (7 real columns): [3.19 1.61 1.02 0.74 0.4  0.03 0.  ]  variance explained by the 1st: 46%
# covariances km/liters/$ (different scales): diagonal [5234115.  643759. 1745617.]
# age and consumption: r +0.598;  partial given route -0.011;  r(age, city) +0.669  r(city, consumption) +0.899
# outlier, no relationship: r +0.015 → +0.570;  Spearman +0.039 → +0.170
# outlier, with relationship: r +0.894 → +0.250;  Spearman +0.901 → +0.642
# 15 trucks: truck age / license plate letter r = +0.48 (500 trucks: +0.01)

Everything matches the simple version: the liters-dollars pair as the multicollinearity case, age and consumption that stop being correlated once you condition on the route, the outlier that takes r from 0.02 to 0.57 (and Spearman only to 0.17) or from 0.89 to 0.25, and the license plate letter that with 15 trucks "correlates" 0.48 with age. The last two eigenvalues of , almost 0, give away the nearly exact dependencies among km, liters and dollars.

§10 · Checklist

Before you trust a correlation

  • Scatter plot drawn (and the scatter-plot matrix if there are several columns).
  • Convention of versus and of rows versus columns (rowvar) checked.
  • Pearson and Spearman compared; if they differ, look for outliers or curvature.
  • Confidence interval (Fisher or bootstrap) as well as the value; careful with n < 30.
  • If many pairs were explored, a multiple-comparisons correction and confirmation on new data.
  • Possible confounding variables (route, truck model, season) measured and controlled: partial correlation or comparison by group.
  • Sample selection reviewed: which trucks are missing and why.
  • For models: VIF or condition number of ; drop or combine redundant columns.
  • Computation in two passes or online with Welford, with the origins subtracted in float64.

§11 · Worked example

Eight trucks, a table and an r of 0.92

The numbers from idea 1 and idea 2 of the simple version, computed by hand: covariance, correlation, units, line, Spearman and confidence interval.

The situation. The dispatch manager wants to know whether it's worth charging a load surcharge: do the more heavily loaded trucks really burn more, how much more, and how much can you trust 8 trucks?

Example map

The 8 trucks from idea 1 of the simple version: average load in tonnes and consumption in L/100 km. We compute by hand the covariance, the correlation, what happens when the units change, the line and its r², the Spearman correlation and how much to trust an r computed from only 8 trucks.

  1. The means.
  2. Deviations and products: the table.
  3. The covariance.
  4. The standard deviations and r.
  5. Switching tonnes for kilograms.
  6. The line, r² and what it's worth in dollars.
  7. Spearman with the ranks.
  8. How much to trust r with 8 trucks?

  1. The means

    In words

    Everything is measured relative to the center of each column, so the first thing is the mean of the load and the mean of the consumption: the cross in the chart.

    The math

    Where does the data come from?

    They are the average load over a month (tonnes per trip) and the average consumption (liters per 100 km) of 8 trucks in the fleet. is read "x bar" and is the mean of column ; the mean consumption, , is in L/100 km.

  2. Deviations and products: the table

    In words

    For each truck: how far it is from the mean in load () and in consumption (), and their product, which is the signed area of the rectangle from idea 1. The last two columns are for the standard deviations.

    The data

    truck
    1627−9−5458125
    2930−6−212364
    31129−4−312169
    41433−11−111
    516311−1−111
    619354312169
    7213664243616
    824359327819
    sum1202560013026874

    A free check

    The deviations of a column always add up to 0 (what some trucks are above the mean is balanced by the ones below). If it doesn't come out 0, the mean is wrong. The products, on the other hand, don't add up to 0: only trucks 4 and 5 give a negative value, and just −1 each.

  3. The covariance

    The math

    Why n − 1 = 7?

    For the same reason as in the variance of topic 7: the deviations are measured from the sample's own means, which are "glued" to the data, and that makes the products a little smaller than they would be with the true means. Dividing by instead of makes up for it on average. Dividing by 8 would give 16.25. The units are those of times those of : tonnes × L/100 km.

    What it means: positive, so load and consumption move together. The 18.57 by itself doesn't say whether the relationship is strong or weak: it depends on the units (step 5).

  4. The standard deviations and r

    In words

    To remove the units, the covariance is divided by the standard deviation of each column. It's the same as computing the covariance of the z's.

    The math

    Why does the second form give the same result?

    The three (the covariance's and the two variances' inside the square roots) cancel out, so . That is exactly the formula for the cosine of the angle between the 8-component arrows and (topic 2): dot product divided by the product of the lengths.

    What it means: a very strong relationship. The two deviation arrows form an angle of : they point almost the same way.

  5. Switching tonnes for kilograms

    The math (each is multiplied by 1,000)

    What it means: the covariance is multiplied by the same 1,000 as the data, and so is the standard deviation; in the ratio it cancels out. r doesn't change with any change of scale or origin (as long as the sign isn't flipped).

  6. The line, r² and what it's worth in dollars

    In words

    The least-squares line that predicts consumption from load has slope "covariance divided by the variance of x", and it goes through the cross of the means.

    The math

    Where does each number come from?

    is liters per 100 km per tonne; would be the consumption of an empty truck according to the line (24.7 L/100 km), an extrapolation because no truck in the table carries less than 6 t. The 1,000 comes from driving 100,000 km a year, which is 1,000 stretches of 100 km; the 1.65 is the price of diesel in $/L. r² is the share of the variance of consumption explained by the line: , which in a regression with a single column equals r squared.

    What it means: each extra tonne of average load costs about $800 of diesel a year for a truck that drives 100,000 km. 85% of the differences in consumption among these 8 trucks go in line with the load; the remaining 15% comes from other things (route, driver, maintenance). Careful: this is an observed relationship, not an experiment (§6).

  7. Spearman with the ranks

    In words

    Each value is replaced by its rank within its column. Trucks 6 and 8 tie in consumption (35, ranks 6th and 7th), so both get the average rank, 6.5.

    The data

    truckrank in loadrank in consumption
    11100
    223−11
    33211
    445−11
    55411
    666.5−0.50.25
    778−11
    886.51.52.25
    sum363607.5

    And the 6?

    It's Spearman's shortcut: when the ranks are 1, 2, …, n with no ties, the Pearson r of the ranks simplifies to that formula (the 6 and the come from the sums and from 1 to n). With ties it's only an approximation: the Pearson r computed with the 6.5 ranks gives 0.910, which is what scipy.stats.spearmanr returns.

    What it means: almost the same as Pearson (0.923): there are no outliers inflating r and the relationship is roughly a straight line. If the two differed a lot, you would have to look at the cloud.

  8. How much to trust r with 8 trucks?

    In words

    With another 8 trucks you'd get a different r. Two questions: could an r this large come out with no real relationship at all? And between which values, reasonably, is the correlation of the whole fleet?

    The math

    Where does each constant come from?

    If there were no relationship at all in the fleet, the statistic would follow a Student's t with degrees of freedom (2 are lost to the two means); is the probability of a this large or larger by chance, and it comes from a table or from scipy.stats.t.sf. For the interval, Fisher showed that is nearly normal with standard deviation ; 1.96 is the value that leaves the central 95% of a normal; undoes the transformation.

    What it means: it's very unlikely to be a coincidence (1 in 900), but the fleet's correlation could be anywhere between 0.63 and 0.99: with 8 trucks you know the sign and that it's strong, not much more. And none of this says that load causes consumption, even though here physics backs it up.

ejemplo.py · reproduces the numbers above

import math
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from cor import rangos

x = np.array([6, 9, 11, 14, 16, 19, 21, 24.]); y = np.array([27, 30, 29, 33, 31, 35, 36, 35.]); n = 8
dx, dy = x - x.mean(), y - y.mean()
print("1. means", x.sum(), "/ 8 =", x.mean(), "  ", y.sum(), "/ 8 =", y.mean())
print("2. dx", dx.tolist(), " dy", dy.tolist(), "\n   dx·dy", (dx * dy).tolist(), " dx²", (dx**2).tolist(), " dy²", (dy**2).tolist())
print("   sums", dx.sum(), dy.sum(), (dx * dy).sum(), (dx**2).sum(), (dy**2).sum())
c = (dx * dy).sum() / (n - 1); sx, sy = math.sqrt((dx**2).sum() / 7), math.sqrt((dy**2).sum() / 7)
print("3. cov", round(c, 4), " with n instead of n − 1:", (dx * dy).sum() / n)
r = c / (sx * sy); print("4. sx", round(sx, 4), " sy", round(sy, 4), " sx·sy", round(sx * sy, 4), " r", round(r, 4), " √(268·74)", round(math.sqrt(268 * 74), 2))
print("5. in kg: cov", round(c * 1000, 1), " sx", round(sx * 1000, 1), " r", round(c * 1000 / (sx * 1000 * sy), 4))
b = 130 / 268; a = y.mean() - b * x.mean()
print("6. slope", round(b, 4), " intercept", round(a, 3), " r²", round(r * r, 4), " 100,000 km:", round(b * 1000, 1), "L", "$" + str(round(b * 1000 * 1.65, 1)),
      "  20 t truck:", round(a + b * 20, 2))
rx, ry = rangos(x), rangos(y); d = rx - ry
print("7. ranks x", rx.tolist(), " y", ry.tolist(), " d", d.tolist(), " Σd²", (d**2).sum(),
      " 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n²−1))", round(1 - 6 * (d**2).sum() / (n * (n * n - 1)), 4), " Pearson of the ranks", round(np.corrcoef(rx, ry)[0, 1], 4), " scipy", round(stats.spearmanr(x, y).statistic, 4))
t = r * math.sqrt((n - 2) / (1 - r * r)); z = math.atanh(r); h = 1.959964 / math.sqrt(n - 3)
print("8. t", round(t, 3), " p", round(2 * stats.t.sf(t, n - 2), 5), " atanh(r)", round(z, 4), " 1/√5", round(1 / math.sqrt(5), 4), " h", round(h, 4),
      " [", round(z - h, 4), round(z + h, 4), "] → [", round(math.tanh(z - h), 3), round(math.tanh(z + h), 3), "]")

What would change in a real system

  • More trucks, and by group: the slope per tonne depends on the route and the truck model; compute it within each group.
  • Trip by trip, not monthly averages: correlating group averages inflates r (ecological fallacy); with per-trip data, r is usually quite a bit lower.
  • A regression with several columns (load, route, speed, age) instead of a lone correlation, keeping an eye on multicollinearity.
  • An experiment if the decision is expensive: randomly assign loads to comparable trucks for a few weeks.
